trigger_points.location_description: Point in the proximal belly, palpated through the anterior axillary fold against the humeral head with the arm slightly abducted.
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Anterior deltoid pain, then a projection down the posterior arm, dorsal forearm and dorsum of the hand (often described as skipping segments).
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Pain reaching behind the back and combing hair (combined extension-abduction stretch); difficulty with sustained front-carry.
trigger_points.notes: Typically appears as a 'second-layer' source, after other anterior-shoulder muscles' trigger points have been treated.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons Trigger Point Manual -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded shoulder muscle reference document (Donnelly JM, Fernandez-de-las-Penas C, Finnegan M, Freeman JL (eds), Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual, 3rd ed., Wolters Kluwer, 2019)

clinical.function_biomechanics: Flexion and adduction of the arm (returning the abducted arm to the side, forward-and-inward reach); stabilises the humeral head anteriorly at low abduction as part of the conjoint mass; postural holding of loads carried in front.
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: Coracobrachial (subcoracoid-region) bursa between the muscle/conjoint tendon and subscapularis–capsule beneath the coracoid. Adjacent structures — mutual influence: Musculocutaneous nerve within/through it — hypertrophy or heavy eccentric load can irritate it (lateral-forearm paraesthesiae, biceps/brachialis weakness); coracoid impingement region medial to the tendon; short head of biceps fused proximally.

trigger_points.location: TrP in the proximal belly, palpated through the anterior axillary fold against the humeral head with the arm slightly abducted.
trigger_points.referred_pain: Anterior deltoid pain, then a projection down the posterior arm, dorsal forearm and dorsum of the hand (often described as skipping segments); typically appears after other anterior-shoulder muscles’ TrPs are treated — a “second-layer” source.
trigger_points.source: Donnelly JM, Fernández-de-las-Peñas C, Finnegan M, Freeman JL (eds). Travell, Simons & Simons’ Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual. 3rd ed. Wolters Kluwer; 2019. Muscle chapters as named in each section.

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: Into its felt zone: anterior deltoid convergence (infraspinatus, biceps, scaleni, pectorals)
posterior-arm projection overlaps triceps long head, teres major and subscapularis patterns
clinical.movement_restrictions_aggravators: Pain reaching behind the back and combing hair (combined extension–abduction stretch); difficulty with sustained front-carry.
clinical.notes: After successful anterior-shoulder TrP treatment, recurrent anterior pain with dorsal-hand referral → re-examine coracobrachialis before blaming the biceps.
clinical.caveat: Trigger-point locations and referral maps derive from the Travell–Simons clinical-observational tradition, now standardised by Delphi consensus criteria [32] and supported by prevalence and hyperalgesia studies in shoulder pain [30,31]; they are expert-level evidence, not trial-level, and inter-examiner reliability of TrP palpation is moderate. Facet, ACJ and subacromial referral patterns, by contrast, come from experimental provocation in volunteers/patients [33,34,37]. Textbook anatomy is cited at section level; where major texts disagree (segmental levels), the range is given and flagged. Figures and patterns older than 12 months are anatomical/physiological constants and are not considered stale.
